title: Microstructure and tensile behaviors for a medium Mn steel with δ-ferrite phase under different annealing temperatures
abstract: In this experiment, we systematically investigated the microstructure evolution, mechanical properties, and deformation behaviors as functions of annealing temperature using cold-rolled Fe-0.05C–6Mn–1Al-1.5Si steel. Almost all annealed specimens are composed of the equiaxed and granular α-ferrite (α) grains due to recrystallization, reversed austenite (γ) grains because of reversed transformation from deformed martensite, and fibrous δ-ferrite (δ) grains only undergoing recovery during intercritical annealing except for 760 °C. It is interesting that several annealing twins are formed within γ grains. The outstanding combination of strength and ductility is obtained for annealing at 740 °C. The tensile strength and total elongation are 980 MPa and 32.1%, which are attributed to the ultrafine grains and optimal TRIP effect associated with rational γ content and stability. A phenomenon that yield point elongation (YPE) gradually shortens with increased γ content and decreased γ stability is observed. What's more, the mechanism that active α′ formation can promote the improvement of work hardening rate and further curtail YPE is verified using deep-cryogenic treatment. Based on SEM observation, microscopic strain of δ grains appears nearly consistent with matrix (α and γ grains) during tensile process, although δ phase presents as fibrous morphology with coarse size.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Medium Mn steels, as one of 3rd generation advanced high-strength steels, are currently important candidate in the development and application of automotive materials to meet requirement for automobile lightning, and thus reducing production cost, improving fuel economy and vehicle safety [ 1 , 2 ]. In general, medium Mn steels containing α-ferrite (α) and austenite (γ) phases tend to exert the excellent combination of strength and ductility [ 3 ], because the formation of martensite (α′) from γ during the plastic deformation usually retards necking due to localized work hardening, i.e., transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect [ 4 ].

It is crucial for metals such as steel [ 5 ] and aluminum alloy [ 6 , 7 ] subjected by cold deformation to conduct annealing treatment for the applied purpose. To date, the influences of initial α′ microstructure, annealing conditions such as temperature, time, cooling, and heating rates [ 8 , 9 ], and alloying elements (C, Mn, Si, Al [ 10 ]) and cold-rolling [ 11 ] on the microstructure evolution, tensile property, deformation behavior and fracture of medium Mn steels have been studied. Cold-rolled medium Mn steel usually consists of equiaxed and granular microstructures of α and γ grains due to recrystallization and reversed transformation during intercritical annealing (IA), respectively. However, as-quenched α′ often transforms into lath-shaped α and γ phases during IA, which are inherited from the original α′ lath. Mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of medium Mn steels are closely related to the content and stability of γ [ 3 ], size and morphology of grain [ 12 ], dislocation distribution [ 13 ], particle precipitation [ 14 ], and strain rate [ 15 ].

Medium Mn steels treated by cold-rolling and IA always expose a shortcoming of surface quality, for instance, discontinuous yielding with a larger yield point elongation [ 16–21 ]. In addition, this behavior was also found in lath-shaped microstructure of medium Mn steels with or warm-rolling and quenching before IA [ 22 , 23 ]. The explanations on discontinuous yielding in medium Mn steels include the inhomogeneous strain distribution between α and γ phases [ 18 ], the rapid increase of mobile dislocations in α/γ interfaces [ 17 ], the C segregation at α/γ phase boundaries [ 16 ], the interaction of solute C atoms and dislocations in α phase [ 21 ]. Even so, there is no an objective interpretation for formation of discontinuous yielding in medium Mn steels to be recognized universally.

δ-ferrite (δ) phase was noted and investigated in several medium Mn steels with addition of Al (and Si) element [ 24–28 ]. Lee et al. [ 27 ] discovered an inhomogeneous strain distribution between δ, γ and α′ phases in a hot-rolled steel, and noted that δ grains are deformed at a higher rate than the other two due to low hardness. However, there is no strain partitioning can be found between δ and γ phases in medium Mn steel [ 24 ]. Failure of medium Mn steel starts with crack initiation at the interfaces of δ and matrix (α and γ phases), and then cracks preferably propagate into the brittle δ layers [ 25 , 26 ].

However, it is acknowledged that much less attention is concentrated on the influence of α′ transformed from γ on the yield point elongation in medium Mn steel [ 16 ]. This work singly changes γ content by introducing deep-cryogenic treatment to investigate the yield point elongation. Besides, strain of δ phase and matrix in cold-rolled and annealed steel is unclear during the tensile testing. The combination of SEM and tension were used to study the microscopic strain between fibrous δ phase and matrix in detail. Consequently, the current work aims to investigate the effect of annealing temperature on the microstructure evolution, mechanical properties, and deformation behaviors of cold-rolled Fe-0.05C–6Mn–1Al-1.5Si steel with δ phase.

sections.heading: Experimental procedure
paragraphs: A chemical composition of Fe-0.055C-5.9Mn-1.0Al-1.55Si (wt.%) steel was processed. The detailed processes of cast and hot-rolling were introduced in previous work [ 29 ]. Cold rolling was conducted to an eventual thickness of 1.25 mm with a reduction of 50%. The austenite-start temperature (620 °C) of the cold-rolled steel was determined using a DIL-805 A/D type dilatometer. The cold-rolled plates were annealed from 660 °C to 760 °C in 20 °C intervals for 3 min followed by water cooling in a muffle furnace.

The microstructures of the experimental steel were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) by a spatial step size of 0.05 μm. The 50 μm foils for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation were prepared in a mixture of 5% HClO 4  and 95% CH 3 CH 2 OH at −20 °C. The chemical compositions of grains were determined by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) in the TEM. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) data were collected in the angle range of 40–100° with a scanning speed of 4°/min. The volume fraction of γ was determined with the integrated intensities of (200)α, (211)α, (200)γ, (220)γ and (311)γ diffraction peaks and the following method [ 30 ]:

All samples apart from ones for TEM observation were mechanically ground and then electro-polished using a 90 mL CH 3 COOH and 10 mL HClO 4  solution with voltage of 30 V for 30 s. Tensile specimens with a 25 mm gauge length parallel to the rolling direction were machined, and the uniaxial tensile tests with a constant strain rate of 2 × 10 −3 s −1  were carried out at room temperature. Furthermore, micro-hardness measurements were implemented by Vickers-hardness tester with a holding time of 15 s.

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs:
The microstructures of medium Mn steel with hot- and cold-rolling are characterized by SEM in  Fig. 1 
                      . The microstructures of hot-rolled sample consist of lath-shaped as-quenched martensite (α′) and fibrous δ-ferrite (δ) bands extending along rolling direction. By comparison, it is a remarkable difference in morphology except for fibrous δ as usual. As-quenched α′ laths are regular and straight, whereas deformed α′ is composed of numerous deformation bands.

Figure 2 
                       presents microstructures of annealed samples ranging from 680 °C to 760 °C using SEM and TEM. As for sample annealed at 680 °C, the globular carbide particles (marked by white rectangles) were formed and undissolved at low IA temperature. In addition, these carbide particles intensively distribute within δ grains and at boundaries of microstructure originated from α'. Even more noteworthy, the coarse structure (black rectangle) is found in several regions on account of lower IA temperature, which descends from the initial α′ in  Fig. 1 b. When annealing temperature is above 680 °C in  Fig. 2 b–e, the ultrafine-grained structures evaluated from deformed α′ are formed and increasingly evident due to recrystallization and reversed transformation. The fibrous microstructure of δ phase seems to be unchanged during annealing with not higher than 740 °C, whereas δ recrystallization in annealed sample at 760 °C is noticed and amplified in the inset of  Fig. 2 e, and the equiaxed grain is approximately 0.8 μm in size. Recrystallization from deformed δ microstructure during IA in medium Mn steels has been rarely reported up to now.  Figure 2 f reveals the micrograph of annealed sample at 740 °C as example by TEM. The grain size of the equiaxed and granular microstructures in sample annealed at 740 °C is below 0.5 μm on average.

Depictions of the EDS results for sample annealed at 740 °C in the form of quantitative composition maps are presented in  Fig. 3 
                      . Microstructural features of annealed sample using secondary electron image and bright-field image with Mn concentration are presented in  Fig. 3 a and d. The development of γ grains is independent on the partitioning of Mn and C atoms from α, thus segregation of atoms mentioned above can be utilized to distinguish phase. The Mn concentrations are ~4.8 wt% in α grains and 8.78 wt% in γ grain for sample annealed at 740 °C in  Fig. 3 d. The mappings also indicate that Al atoms are rich in δ grains rather than in α and γ grains, and Si atoms occupy almost all the region homogeneously.

Figure 4 
                      a describes engineering stress–strain curves at room temperature of samples annealed from 660 °C to 760 °C, in which a common phenomenon, i.e., yield point elongation, is marked by a dotted rectangle. The mechanical properties such as yield strength, tensile strength, and total elongation, will be discussed in section  4.2 . The variation of micro-hardness of annealed samples using a hardness tester with a load of 300 g was stated in  Fig. 4 b. The hardness gradually decreases from 299 HV to 279 HV and then increases up to 282 HV, when the temperature increases from 660 °C to 760 °C. Increasingly full recovery and recrystallization of deformed microstructures during annealing process are responsible for the reduction in hardness. Meanwhile, the sudden rebound in hardness appearing at 760 °C must be related the fresh α′ transformed from reducing thermal stability of γ during cooling process.

sections.heading: Reversed transformation and recrystallization
paragraphs:
In order to delicately explore microstructure evolution of deformed α′, the specimen annealed at 720 °C was characterized by TEM.  Figure 5 
                         a presents bright-field micrograph with high density of dislocation regions, in which a region marked by yellow circle is measured as body-centered cubic (bcc) structure. The existence of regions with massive dislocation tangles is attributed to inactive recovery during IA. There are two types of grain morphologies regarding γ, which are equiaxed microstructure indicated by yellow arrow and granular microstructure by white in  Fig. 5 b, and the sizes of γ grains are approximately 0.3 μm. Meanwhile, the majority of region is filled with equiaxed and granular grains in  Fig. 5 c.

Taking EBSD analysis,  Fig. 6 
                         a–c exhibit the phase maps of γ grains (red) upon the image quality maps for annealed samples ranging from 720 °C to 760 °C. Evidently, the equiaxed and granular γ grains disperse in ferrite grains described uncolored regions. The reason why γ grains developed with two microstructures proposed above, is because recrystallization process restricts the developmental space of γ grains. The γ is aggregated existence along high-angle boundaries in  Fig. 6 d. Mechanism of preferential nucleation along high angle boundaries is that it provides low barrier for nucleation [ 31 ], such as higher density of dislocations, elemental segregation and higher misorientation angles.  Figure 6 e displays the random orientation of γ on account of the inverse pole figure, and this phenomenon results from nucleation afresh. According to  Fig. 6 f, the recrystallization and substructure occupy the majority of deformed α′ regions prior to annealing, yet δ phase only consists of substructure due to recovery during annealing at 740 °C.

Figure 7 
                          presents bright-field images of specimens annealed at 720 °C and 740 °C. Thickness of twin lamella were measured to be diverse as 0.04 
                            
                               ∼ 
                            
                         0.2 μm by TEM. Interestingly, three parallel and adjacent annealing twins with small size intersect with a central twin running through the whole grain at an angle of 110° in the inset of  Fig. 7 a. The formation and growth of annealing twin rely on stacking fault energy in a way, and the motion of grain boundaries due to stacking fault of atoms causes to formation of twins on specific plates during grain growth process [ 32 ]. Certainly, twin boundaries can refine grains, thus which improves mechanical properties. In fact, the annealing twin in medium Mn steels without micro-alloy elements has been scarcely reported [ 26 ].

sections.heading: TRIP effect and mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The volume fraction of γ measured by XRD in annealed samples ranging from 660 °C to 760 °C is exhibited in  Fig. 8 
                         . Diffraction peaks of γ become increasingly stronger with rising temperature in  Fig. 8 a. Volume fraction of γ rapidly increase from 1.2% to 14.7% occurring at 700 °C and then gradually develop until 23.1%. The mechanical properties of these annealed samples are concluded in  Fig. 9 
                         . With the rising of annealing temperature, the yield strength dramatically decreases, and then remains approximately unchanged until 740 °C followed by decreasing once again. Nevertheless, the tensile strength exhibits a reduced trend until 700 °C followed by rising. It is confirmed that increasingly active recrystallization is primarily responsible for variation of yield strength. Additionally, the rebounds of tensile strength starting at 720 °C must be due to abundant α′ formation induced by stress. Even though the volume fraction of γ increases continuously, the total elongation still increases at first and appears a decreased trend, so does the product of strength and elongation (PSE) value. The optimal combination of mechanical properties is partly attributed to the optimum content and stability of γ, which provides a moderate TRIP effect. The ultrafine α and γ grains also contribute to the improvement of mechanical properties to some degree.

There are evident differences on deformation behavior and mechanical properties of samples annealed at 740 °C and 760 °C as shown in  Figs. 4a and 9 . As for these two samples, the work hardening rate (WHR) curves and variation of volume fraction of γ with true strain are plotted in  Fig. 10 
                         . Strain hardening behavior of medium Mn steel is closely related to α′ transformation influenced by content and mechanical stability of γ. An exponential function proposed by Knijf et al. [ 33 ] was used to describe the evolution of γ content with true strain:

The lower  B  value is, the higher mechanical stability of γ is. The factor of stability  B  are 12.4 and 22.6 for two samples annealed at 740 °C and 760 °C, which indicates that mechanical stability of the latter is clearly lower. This evident difference in mechanical stability can be attributed to grain size and Mn concentration in γ grains. The size and concentration are 0.289 μm and 9.8 ± 1.2wt% for sample annealed at 740 °C, whereas 0.33 μm and 8.2 ± 0.6wt% are for the other. The whole WHR curve is divided into three stages in  Fig. 10 a, where the primary variety lies in the second stage. The WHR of sample annealed at 740 °C increases to ~2000 MPa at first, and then this stable hardening process continues to 0.18 in strain. This process is associated with slow reducing of γ, indicating that the γ to α′ transformation was occurred steadily and uniformly (i.e., the stable and sustained TRIP effect). By contrast, the WHR of sample annealed at 760 °C fluctuates at ~1250 MPa firstly corresponding to yield point elongation in  Fig. 4 a, and then reaches up to a large value followed by a drop abruptly. The fact that volume fraction of γ reduces at a relatively faster rate can explain the higher WHR value.

sections.heading: Active TRIP effect and yield point elongation
paragraphs:
Compared with γ grains, α grains with a low density of dislocations and poor concentrations of C and Mn are deemed as soft phase and easily deform at the early stage of tensile, resulting in discontinuous yielding of medium Mn steels [ 18 ]. Ding et al. [ 20 ] noted that inhomogeneous deformation produced by strain softening and hardening mainly causes to discontinuous yielding. However, the sample annealed at 660 °C without almost γ phase (in  Fig. 8 b) still presents the largest yield point elongation (YPE). In other words, one sample with only one phase (α) shows severely discontinuous yielding.  Figure 11 
                         a and b exhibit the quantitative measurement of YPE in engineering strain for annealed samples from 660 °C to 740 °C. From the engineering stress–strain curves, YPE was measured by subtracting the strain at the lower yield point from initial strain point of uniform strain hardening appearance. YPE of these samples are 4.0%, 2.2%, 2.0%, 1.5% and 1.3% with rising annealing temperature sequentially.  Figure 11 c and d shows γ grain size distribution and Mn concentration in γ grains for samples annealed at 720 °C and 740 °C. Note that the differences of grain size and Mn concentration between samples have an important influence on the γ stability. In general, γ stability decreases with increasing temperature on account of grain size and Mn content. A few studies [ 17 , 18 ] suggested that γ to α′ transformation is indeed able to occur in the stage of YPE and enhance WHR, and this phase transformation induced by strain was also confirmed in our experiment as shown in  Fig. 10 b. Shen et al. [ 34 ] stated that γ to α′ transformation doesn't directly provide strain hardening for Lüders band propagation. There is a mechanism leading to the continuous decreasing in YPE in fact. Unfortunately, much less attention has been stated the influence of γ to α′ transformation on YPE so far.

To explore the mechanism that active γ to α′ transformation induced by strain can enhance WHR and shorten YPE, a method of deep-cryogenic treatment (DCT) was innovatively introduced as shown in  Fig. 12 
                         a. Plates annealed at 720 °C and 740 °C were accepted water cooling at 25 °C for 5s at first and deep-cryogenic treatment at −196 °C for 28h taking liquid nitrogen. Tsuchida et al. [ 35 ] suggested that discontinuous yielding in carbon steels is affected by various microstructural factors such as ferrite grain size, temperature, and carbon concentration. It should be especially illustrated that there is no variation in grain size and chemical concentration during DCT process.

Figure 12 b and c presents volume fraction of γ and yielding behavior in samples after DCT. For one thing, the volume fractions of γ decrease from 18.5% to 16.3% for sample annealed at 720 °C and from 20.3% to 14.9% for one at 740 °C. For another, stability of γ on average becomes indirectly stronger due to α′ transformation from γ with lower stability during DCT. The corresponding YPE of sample annealed at 720 °C extends from 1.5% to 2.4% in engineering strain, and the value from 1.3% to 2.1% is for the other. The reason why the YPE of samples with DCT become prolongation is that decreasing α′ transformation from γ lessens in the stage of YPE. The α′ transformation should not have a critical role on the absence of discontinuous yielding, but rather affect the YEP due to the increase of local work hardening rate. Previous works [ 12 , 18 ] conducted on medium Mn steels subjected to cold-rolling and intercritical annealing reported that active TRIP leads to the improvement of strain hardening rate and accelerates the propagation of Lüders band at the early stage of yielding. Hence, we can summarize that α′ formation from γ with increasing content and decreasing stability is able to heighten WHR in the initial stage of plastic deformation and shorten YPE.

sections.heading: Microstructure and strain of δ-ferrite phase
paragraphs:
The addition of Al (and Si) element is responsible for the formation and stabilization of δ phase, which is a result of non-equilibrium cooling during solidification.  Figure 13 
                         a displays optical micrograph of cold-rolled steel, the microstructure model of δ and matrix was processed by Image J software in  Fig. 13 b. The fibrous δ phase was expressed with bright regions, and its volume fraction was calculated as about 21%. Micro-hardness values of δ and matrix (α and γ) in sample annealed at 740 °C were measured as 274 ± 3HV and 287 ± 4HV using a hardness tester with a load of 25g, respectively. In order to further certain several features of δ in annealed samples, bright-filed image and KAM image of sample annealed at 740 °C are presented in  Fig. 13 c–d. The KAM parameter is the average misorientation of all adjacent points regarding a given kernel [ 36 ]. Thus, the KAM measure can be used as an index to evaluating crystal defects, such as geometrically necessary dislocations. The approximate density of dislocations is found in matrix and δ phase on average, when the sample was annealed at 740 °C.

The combination of SEM and tension were considered to investigate the microscopic strain between fibrous δ phase and matrix. As shown in  Fig. 14 
                         a, the technical route in detail contains annealing at 740 °C, grinding & polishing of observational surface, indentation mark taking a Vickers-hardness tester, feature of initial position by SEM, tensile deformation with 5%, 9%, 13% and 17% in engineering strain, and characterization after tensile by SEM.  Figure 14 b and c shows microscopic changes between δ and matrix in specimen annealed at 740 °C with increasing strain up to 17%. Consequently, we conclude that fibrous δ grains deform with matrix in this treated steel during tensile process. This case is consistent with deformation of phases in cold-rolled medium Mn steel tested by Sun et al. [ 24 ]. According to  Fig. 13 a, the δ and matrix are arranged alternatively with each other along normal direction to form layered structure, which is similar to laminated structure. When the layered structure is deformed during tensile testing parallel to the elongated direction, it is necessary for the δ and matrix to keep the same strain rate to maintain the macro-strain compatibility.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
This work concentrates on the influence of annealing temperature on the microstructural development, mechanical properties, and deformation behaviors (including strain hardening, yield point elongation and microscopic strain) in a cold-rolled Fe-0.05C–6Mn–1Al-1.5Si steel. The critical results can be summarized as follows. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Formation of the equiaxed and granular shapes of α-ferrite and austenite grains attributes to the active recrystallization and reversed transformation from deformed martensite, respectively, whereas recrystallization of fibrous δ-ferrite grains is just discovered through annealing at 760 °C. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            An increase in annealing temperature from 660 °C to 760 °C boosts the volume fraction of austenite from 1.2% to 23.1%. Meanwhile, the diverse austenite twins ranging 0.04 
                                  
                                     ∼ 
                                  
                               0.2 μm in width are also formed during intercritical annealing. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            This steel exhibits a significantly excellent combination of strength and ductility at 740 °C, with tensile strength of 980 MPa, total elongation of 32.1% and PSE of 31.5 GPa%, which originates from ultrafine grains and stable TRIP effect. Besides, the decreasing in mechanical stability of austenite at 760 °C leads to reduction of comprehensive performance. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            A clear relationship between increased TRIP effect below 760 °C and decreased yield point elongation is determined. The introduction of deep-cryogenic treatment has been directly demonstrated that active martensite transformation from austenite improves strain hardening rate and shortens the yield point elongation. 
                         
                         
                            (5) 
                            There is no strain distribution behavior between δ-ferrite and matrix to maintain the macro-strain compatibility during tensile deformation, even if δ-ferrite is deemed as fibrous morphology.
